### Step 1. Identify the structure of the Lie algebra

The given Lie algebra is
$$\mathfrak{g} = \left\{X(a,u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}0&-a&u\\ a&0&v\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix} : a,u,v\in\mathbb{R}\right\}.$$

Introduce the basis
$$J=X(1,0,0)=\begin{bmatrix}0&-1&0\\1&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad P_1=X(0,1,0)=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&1\\0&0&0\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix},\quad P_2=X(0,0,1)=\begin{bmatrix}0&0&0\\0&0&1\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}.$$

### Step 2. Compute the commutators

For $X=X(a,u,v)$ and $X'=X(a',u',v')$, direct matrix multiplication gives
$$[X,X']=X\bigl(0,\; a'v-av',\; au'-a'u\bigr).$$

Applying this to the basis:
$$[J,P_1]=P_2,\qquad [J,P_2]=-P_1,\qquad [P_1,P_2]=0.$$

These are precisely the structure equations of $\mathfrak{se}(2)$, the Lie algebra of the **special Euclidean group** $SE(2)$.

### Step 3. Exhibit the candidate Lie group

Consider the matrix Lie group
$$SE(2)=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}\cos\theta&-\sin\theta&x\\ \sin\theta&\cos\theta&y\\0&0&1\end{bmatrix}:\theta\in\mathbb{R},\;x,y\in\mathbb{R}\right\}=SO(2)\ltimes\mathbb{R}^2,$$
the group of orientation-preserving rigid motions (isometries) of the Euclidean plane.

### Step 4. Verify the Lie algebra matches

An element of $SE(2)$ has the block form $\begin{bmatrix}R&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ with $R\in SO(2)$, $t\in\mathbb{R}^2$. Its Lie algebra consists of matrices $\begin{bmatrix}A&b\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ where $A\in\mathfrak{so}(2)=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}0&-a\\a&0\end{bmatrix}\right\}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^2$. This is exactly
$$\mathfrak{se}(2)=\left\{\begin{bmatrix}0&-a&u\\a&0&v\\0&0&0\end{bmatrix}:a,u,v\in\mathbb{R}\right\}=\mathfrak{g}.$$

### Step 5. Confirm via the exponential map

For $X(a,u,v)=\begin{bmatrix}A&b\\0&0\end{bmatrix}$ with $A=\begin{bmatrix}0&-a\\a&0\end{bmatrix}$, the matrix exponential is
$$\exp X=\begin{bmatrix}e^A & \displaystyle\int_0^1 e^{sA}\,ds\; b\\ 0&1\end{bmatrix}.$$

Since $e^A=\begin{bmatrix}\cos a&-\sin a\\\sin a&\cos a\end{bmatrix}\in SO(2)$ and the upper-right block is a vector in $\mathbb{R}^2$, we have $\exp X\in SE(2)$. The group $SE(2)$ is connected, so it is generated by exponentials; hence $\operatorname{Lie}(SE(2))=\mathfrak{g}$.

### Conclusion

The Lie group is
$$\boxed{G = SE(2) = SO(2)\ltimes\mathbb{R}^2},$$
the **special Euclidean group of the plane** — the group of orientation-preserving isometries of $\mathbb{R}^2$, realized as $3\times 3$ real matrices $\begin{bmatrix}R&t\\0&1\end{bmatrix}$ with $R\in SO(2)$ and $t\in\mathbb{R}^2$.
